newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada union hopeful of Ford Canada deal.
newsitem.headline: Canada union hopeful of Ford Canada deal.

text.p: The Canadian Auto Workers union voiced optimism late on Monday that a contract deal with Ford Motor Co. of Canada Ltd. could be reached on Tuesday after the automaker presented an economic offer Monday evening that matches the deal sought by the union.

CAW President Buzz Hargrove said the offer by Ford appears to include all the contract language laid out in the pattern agreement forged recently with the Canadian units of Chrysler Corp. and General Motors Corp.
"We now have the pattern," said Hargrove. "We want to drive now to try to do this thing by tomorrow."

Ford chief negotiator Donald McKenzie said work still needs to be done to settle local issues but he is confident a contract can be reached before the union's 7 P.M. EST (2400 GMT) Wednesday strike deadline.
"I'm confident that having tabled this agreement and having matched the pattern, we can get there," said McKenzie.

Hargrove said the union, which represents about 11,700 Ford workers, would spend the night checking the offer's language to ensure there are no errors or omissions and meeting with company negotiators to iron out several outstanding local concerns.
The two sides remained at odds over skilled trades and office work issues as well as working conditions at Ford's truck and van assembly plant in Oakville, Ontario.
Hargrove said the local hangups would not stand in the way of a deal.
"These are not unresolvable issues, these are not issues (McKenzie) is going to put the operation in the ditch over," said Hargrove.

The pattern deal offers the union protection from outsourcing, or contracting out jobs, ensures minimum health and safety and employment standards and gives workers improved benefits and a 10.2 percent wage and cost of living increase over three years.

Hargrove said he was disappointed that Ford included several unexpected demands with its offer, including proposals to alter contracts currently in place which govern leaves of absences for union staff, overpayment recovery, vacation time and a temporary part-time workforce.
The union said it would consider the demands, which Hargrove said had been rejected at the local bargaining level.
"If he couldn't get them at the local table he's certainly not going to get them here, unless some of it makes sense," said Hargrove. "We'll look at it, I don't want to reject it out of hand."

In October talks between the union and GM Canada broke down after the company presented its economic offer just hours before the strike deadline. The ensuing 20-day strike by 26,000 GM workers disrupted production across North America.
Ford Canada is a wholly owned unit of Ford Motor Co.
